stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Nutrition researchers often judge the health effects of a diet by asking what replaces a given nutrient when it is removed. In a 2021 analysis of 34 controlled feeding trials, a team led by dietitian Mara Okafor found that replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat lowered LDL cholesterol in nearly every trial ______ replacing saturated fat with refined carbohydrates produced no measurable improvement.
explanation: The text before the blank is a complete sentence, and so is the text after it. The contrast is between the two swaps: polyunsaturated fat helped, but refined carbohydrates did not. So "however" belongs at the start of the second clause. You put the semicolon before "however" to end the first clause, then a comma after it.

B.why: You put the semicolon after "however," which attaches the word to the first clause. That makes it contrast the finding with the sentence before, but that sentence only describes a research method, so there is nothing to contrast. The real contrast, between the two swaps, is then left without a transition.

C.why: You treated "however" like "but" and joined two complete sentences with only commas. That is a comma splice. "However" cannot join clauses, so you need a semicolon or period before it.

D.why: With no punctuation before "however," the two complete sentences run together into a run-on. A strong break has to come before the transition.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Radiocarbon dates from hearths at the Tell Arvani excavation place the site's first occupation at around 6800 BCE, and the excavators initially assumed that its pottery would prove just as old. The earliest layer containing ceramics turned out to be far younger ______ it lay atop nearly two meters of deposits in which not a single potsherd was found.
explanation: The contrast is with the previous sentence: the excavators expected old pottery, but the ceramic layer was much younger. So "however" belongs to the first clause, "The earliest layer... far younger, however." The second clause doesn't contrast with that. It explains it, since the ceramics sat on top of two meters of pottery-free deposits. You put the comma before "however" and the semicolon after it.

A.why: You put "however" at the start of the second clause by default. That makes it contrast "far younger" with the deposits underneath, but the deposits support the claim that the pottery is younger. They don't push against it. The sentence is grammatical, but the transition is attached to the wrong clause.

B.why: You used commas on both sides of "however," so the two complete sentences are joined only by a comma. That is a comma splice.

D.why: You left out the comma before "however." When the transition ends a clause, it has to be set off from the rest of that clause.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Fossil pollen preserved in lake sediments from the Vessa Basin shows oak declining sharply about 4,200 years ago, and many researchers attributed that decline to a regional drought. The charcoal record from the same cores ______ points instead to a series of intense fires that coincided with the arrival of the first farming communities.
explanation: There is no clause boundary here. "The charcoal record from the same cores" is the subject, and "points" is its verb. "However" is interrupting a single clause, so you set it off with a comma on each side.

A.why: You reached for the usual "; however," pattern without checking both sides. The semicolon cuts the subject off from its verb, "points," which leaves a fragment on each side.

C.why: You closed the interruption but never opened it. "However" needs a comma on both sides, and this choice leaves out the one before it.

D.why: You put a semicolon between the subject and its verb. Neither "The charcoal record from the same cores, however" nor "points instead to..." can stand alone as a sentence.

stimulus: The town of Ellery Falls began adding fluoride to its municipal water in 1998, over the objections of a small but vocal group of residents. Those objections never fully disappeared ______ even so, voters rejected three separate ballot measures to repeal the program over the following two decades.
explanation: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences. The contrast is that opposition persisted, yet voters kept the program anyway. So "even so" starts the second clause. You put a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

A.why: You put the semicolon after "even so," which attaches it to the first clause. Objections that never disappeared don't contrast with the sentence before, which already said residents objected. Meanwhile, the real contrast, with the voters keeping the program, is left unmarked.

B.why: You treated "even so" like "but" and joined two complete sentences with commas alone. That is a comma splice.

C.why: With no punctuation before "even so," the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on.

B.why: The long interrupter made you think a new sentence started here. The semicolon leaves "Her maps of the eastern channels" as a fragment, cut off from its verb, "contained."

C.why: You left out the comma before "however," so the transition isn't set off from the subject it interrupts.

D.why: The semicolon separates the subject from "contained," so neither side is a complete sentence. It also leaves the comma after "impossible" without a partner.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Planting cover crops such as winter rye between harvests reduces soil erosion and nitrogen runoff, benefits that field studies have documented for decades. The practice's effect on the following season's cash-crop yields is less clear ______ some trials report modest gains, while others record small losses, depending largely on soil type and rainfall.
explanation: "Though" here is a trailing adverb that contrasts the uncertain yield effect with the well-documented benefits in the previous sentence. It belongs at the end of the first clause, after a comma. Then a semicolon separates that complete clause from the second one, which explains why the yield effect is unclear.

A.why: You moved "though" to the start of the second clause, as if it worked like "however." There it would contrast "less clear" with mixed trial results, but mixed results are the reason the effect is unclear, not a counterpoint to it.

B.why: You joined two complete sentences with commas only. That is a comma splice, and it also leaves unclear which clause "though" belongs to.

D.why: With no break before the comma, the two complete sentences are joined by a comma alone. That is a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Composer Teodor Halm dated almost none of his manuscripts, and his surviving letters rarely mention works in progress. The paper on which his String Quartet no. 3 is written, however, bears a watermark that musicologist Anja Brevik matched to a batch produced by a Leipzig mill in 1841 ______ the quartet cannot have been composed before that year.
explanation: The second clause is a conclusion drawn from the first: the paper dates from 1841, so the quartet can't be older than that. "Therefore" introduces that conclusion, so it starts the second clause. You put a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

A.why: Putting the semicolon after "therefore" attaches it to the first clause. That would mean the watermark match is a consequence of the sentence before, which makes no sense. It also leaves the actual inference, about the composition date, without a transition.

B.why: You treated "therefore" like "so" and joined two complete sentences with commas alone. That is a comma splice.

C.why: With nothing separating the clauses before "therefore," the two sentences run together into a run-on.

stimulus: When cracks appeared in the steel deck of the Corran Street Bridge in 2021, engineers first suspected its expansion joints, which had failed on several bridges of similar design. The joints proved sound ______ inspectors who removed and examined them found no fatigue damage of any kind. The cracking was eventually traced to corroded bearings beneath the deck.
explanation: The contrast is with the previous sentence: engineers suspected the joints, but the joints turned out to be sound. So "however" ends the first clause. The second clause doesn't push back on "sound." It backs it up with the inspectors' findings. You put the comma before "however" and the semicolon after it.

A.why: You put "however" at the start of the second clause from habit. That makes it contrast "proved sound" with "found no fatigue damage," but finding no damage is the evidence that the joints were sound. The grammar works, but the transition is attached to the wrong clause.

C.why: Commas on both sides of "however" leave two complete sentences joined by a comma. That is a comma splice.

D.why: You left out the comma before "however." When the transition ends a clause, it has to be set off from that clause.
